title: Needleburst tiling latency-cost snapshot
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes on a small exploratory benchmark we ran to measure tiling + opportunistic slot behavior on very short, high-cardinality bursts ("needlebursts"). Goal was to capture p50/p95 shifts and immediate $/1k-token implications compared to baseline small-batch/dynbatch paths. This is a lightweight artifact for the console team — not final analytics.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Needleburst pattern: many independent 1–3 token interactions arriving within 100–300ms windows.
- Tiling (slotized GPU tiling) reduces p95 by ~22% for QPS in 50–200 range vs opportunistic small-batch, but raises amortized $/1k tokens by 6–12% depending on slot granularity.
- Best tradeoff for interactive chat-style microcalls observed with tile-size=8 and a 40ms admission hold: maintains p50 ~ stable and p95 improved, cost delta modest.
- Recommendation: surface a toggle in Console ("needleburst-tiling=on/off") with auto-recommendation for workloads that show <5 tokens per request and median inter-arrival <200ms.

Setup (short):
- Cluster: 4x A10G per pool (dedicated experiment cluster), 2 pools: baseline (smallbatch/dynbatch runtime), tiling-enabled pool (slotized runtime).
- Model: rwd-7b-quant (FP16->8-bit hybrid path to be realistic for Hosted/Dedicated); sequence context 32 tokens max.
- Workload generator: synthetic client that emits Poisson arrival bursts with controllable burst size and micro-latency jitter; seed preserved for replay (seed 20260617-needle).
- Measurements captured: p50, p90, p95, p99 latency (ms), end-to-end cost estimate ($ per 1k tokens) from token accounting + amortization model used by billing team.
- Run durations: 10m warmup + 10m steady-state per experiment, repeated 3x.

Key numeric snapshots (median of 3 runs, steady-state):
(Columns: QPS / p50(ms) / p95(ms) / $ per 1k tokens)

Baseline small-batch (dynbatch):
- 25 QPS  /  32ms  /  210ms  /  $1.25
- 100 QPS /  36ms  /  340ms  /  $1.18
- 200 QPS /  45ms  /  520ms  /  $1.12

Tiling (tile-size=8, admission 40ms):
- 25 QPS  /  30ms  /  160ms  /  $1.33
- 100 QPS /  34ms  /  265ms  /  $1.27
- 200 QPS /  42ms  /  455ms  /  $1.19

Observations on numbers:
- p95 improvement most visible at low-to-mid QPS where bursts are sparse but highly concurrent; at very high QPS tiling and baseline converge.
- Cost increase stems from slightly lower packing efficiency when tiles held open for short waits (admission), which prevents perfect fill for other long-running requests.
- p99 shows similar improvement trend but with noisier sampling (we saw p99 reduce 12–18% at 25–100 QPS).

Simple ASCII chart (p95 vs QPS) — smaller is better:
QPS:   25       100      200
Base:  [=====]   [========] [===========]   (210,340,520ms)
Tile:  [====]    [=====]    [==========]    (160,265,455ms)

Latency distribution sketch (p50/p95 spread) — example at 100 QPS:
- Baseline: p50=36ms | p95=340ms  => long right tail, interleaving effects from mixed session types
- Tiling:   p50=34ms | p95=265ms  => similar median, narrower tail (less tail amplification during needlebursts)

Cost amortization notes (how $/1k was computed):
- Billing model used: token charge + GPU amortization per-minute. For these short-run experiments we used per-minute amortization but applied a small penalty (5%) to simulate burst overhead in multi-tenant pools.
- The per-1k charge adjusts with batching efficiency: higher packing reduces per-token GPU time; tiling increased per-token GPU time slightly at low QPS due to admission latency windows.

Microtradeoffs and knobs tested (quick):
- tile-size: 4, 8, 16 — smaller tile reduced cost delta but diminished p95 benefit; tile-size 8 hit a good middle ground.
- admission-hold: 20ms, 40ms, 80ms — very low hold loses most p95 improvement; very high hold increases cost significantly.
- opportunistic-fill: enabled/disabled — when enabled, background opportunistic admits reduced cost at high QPS but slightly increased p99 noise.

Engineer notes / oddities found during runs:
- A single outlier run showed p95 bounce to +80ms vs median — traced to background GC on one host (logs attached in linked PR); re-run cleared it. Keep an eye on host-level noise for p99 narratives.
- Client generator jitter config is sensitive: small changes to inter-arrival jitter move us between "sustained" and "needle" classification. We should standardize a "needleburst" waveform in the synthetic toolkit.

Recommendations for Console collateral / productizing:
1) Add a simple checklist in the workload onboarding flow: "Are your requests <5 tokens on median? Are inter-arrival gaps <200ms?" If yes, recommend needleburst-tiling.
2) Default tile-size=8 plus admission=40ms as a suggested profile in the Console; surface expected p95 reduction and expected $/1k delta as a confidence band (±8–12%).
3) Add telemetry dims for "needleburst_score" (0–100) to automatically suggest tiling when workloads match the profile.
4) Mark the feature with an opt-in banner in the Hosted API UI for initial experiments; track rollback rate and customer-reported quality regressions.

Next steps / follow-ups:
- Run the same sweep on an RTX8000-equivalent pool (for enterprise private environments) — predicted different cost crossover due to different kernel throughput.
- Replay real customer traces (with permission) to validate that synthetic needleburst maps to observed traces.
- Draft a one-pager for Sales describing "needleburst wins vs costs" with two simple charts (p95 vs QPS, $/1k vs QPS).

Notes to self: attach raw CSVs to the PR (see linked_artifacts) and schedule a short sync with console PM (Marta) Monday.
